profiles.meeting_scenario: At an investment bank's macro research division, a senior economist and a research production manager are holding a coordination meeting for a Monday institutional client note and webinar titled "Why inflation stayed low despite tight labor markets: a dual labor market explanation." The note draws on recent work about the flattening of the Phillips curve in the U.S. and Japan, focusing on worker bargaining power, labor supply elasticity in the secondary market, and workforce composition. The agenda is to align on the economist's narrative handoff, the chart pack built from shared labor-market workbooks, what goes into the appendix, and the publication/compliance sequence. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear plan for who delivers what by Thursday and Friday so the note can be published before the client webinar.

members.name: Dr. Elena Cho
members.expertise: Labor economics, inflation dynamics, cross-country macro thematic research
members.background: Former central bank researcher who now leads thematic macro notes for institutional clients and often converts academic arguments into concise market-facing narratives.
members.private_state: She wants the note to preserve the conceptual nuance of the dual labor market story without spending extra time on publication mechanics, and she is trying to avoid another round of last-minute requests that dilute the economics.
hidden_assumptions: "Final draft" means the economics, structure, and headline charts are settled, even if wording, captions, and footnotes still get polished afterward.
When people say the "latest labor-market workbook," they mean her harmonized economist-maintained file with the newest adjustments for U.S./Japan labor-market splits.
"Appendix" means analytic backup for anticipated client questions, mainly model intuition, regression tables, and extra historical charts.
"Sign-off" for a thematic note is effectively her go-ahead once the research logic is locked, with any remaining routing treated as operational follow-through.

members.name: Marcus Hale
members.expertise: Publication workflow, chartbook assembly, compliance routing, research distribution operations
members.background: He has spent years managing sell-side research release processes and is responsible for making sure notes are formatted, sourced, approved, and distributed on schedule using standard production templates.
members.private_state: He is focused on getting the note through compliance cleanly and on time for Monday's client release, while minimizing surprises for design, legal, and distribution teams.
hidden_assumptions: "Final draft" means a publication-ready document that can enter compliance without substantive content gaps, missing source lines, or unresolved exhibits.
The "latest labor-market workbook" means the most recent approved production copy in the shared publishing folder, not an economist's working file.
"Appendix" includes all client-facing support materials needed for publication quality, such as source notes, country definitions, methodology blurbs, and any chart caveats.
"Sign-off" means the formal approval chain is complete in the standard workflow, including the economist and the cross-asset strategy reviewer before compliance routing.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the final draft
misalignment_points.surface_form: "I'll have the final draft by Thursday afternoon."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the substantive macro argument is locked, the key charts are selected, and only light editorial cleanup may remain.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the note is publication-ready on Thursday, with completed captions, source lines, appendix materials, and no meaningful content revisions expected before compliance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use a common publishing phrase that usually signals readiness, and each assumes the other's standard is the obvious professional norm, so the apparent agreement feels routine rather than risky.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'latest' labor-market workbook they will use
misalignment_points.surface_form: "Use the latest labor-market workbook for the payroll split and Japan comparisons."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to her economist-side workbook updated last Friday with hand-adjusted harmonized series for regular versus non-regular workers and revised bargaining-power proxies.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the most recent approved workbook in the production folder, which is an older version already cleared for charting and standardized metadata.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "latest workbook" sounds precise enough in a shared-file environment, and both believe there is an obvious single current version, so neither feels a need to specify the path or timestamp.

misalignment_points.surface_form: "We'll put the extra detail in the appendix."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the appendix is limited to analytic backup: model intuition, a regression robustness table, and one or two historical charts for client questions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the appendix also covers publication support content: source lines, country definitions, chart notes, methodology blurbs, and disclosure-friendly caveats.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Appendices often serve multiple purposes, and both participants are used to their own function of the appendix being taken for granted, so the broad phrase creates false consensus.

misalignment_points.surface_form: "Once we have sign-off, we can send it to compliance Friday morning."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presumes her approval is the meaningful decision point and that any additional routing is administrative and can happen automatically afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presumes sign-off includes the standard formal approvals from both the economist and the cross-asset strategy reviewer in the ticketing workflow before compliance will accept the note.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume the organizational process is already shared knowledge, and because neither is debating the need for compliance itself, the missing assumption about who must approve never gets surfaced.

turns.inner_thought: I want this note to stay centered on the actual economics: the dual labor market explains why headline tightness didn't translate into broad wage pressure. The main story is the split between primary and secondary segments, bargaining power, and composition effects, especially the U.S./Japan comparison. By Thursday afternoon I can have the economics locked, the structure set, and the headline charts chosen. I am not going to spend the rest of the week getting dragged into publication minutiae if we can avoid it.
turns.utterance: For the Monday note and webinar, I want us to keep the frame very clean: why inflation stayed low despite tight labor markets, with the dual labor market story doing the work on the Phillips curve puzzle in the U.S. and Japan. I’ll have the final draft by Thursday afternoon.
